description: Comprehensive 50-Question Physics Question Bank for Diode V-I Characteristics

questions.question: What is the typical barrier potential (knee/cut-in voltage) of a silicon p-n junction diode at room temperature (300 K)?
questions.answer: Approximately 0.7 V
questions.correct_option: Approximately 0.7 V
questions.explanation: Silicon p-n junctions have a built-in potential barrier of approximately 0.6 V to 0.7 V at 300 K.

questions.question: What is the typical knee (threshold) voltage of a germanium p-n junction diode at room temperature?
questions.answer: Approximately 0.3 V
questions.correct_option: Approximately 0.3 V
questions.explanation: Germanium diodes have a smaller bandgap (~0.66 eV), resulting in a lower built-in barrier of approximately 0.2 V to 0.3 V.

questions.question: What happens to the depletion region width when a p-n junction diode is forward biased?
options: The depletion region narrows, lowering the potential barrier
questions.answer: The depletion region narrows, lowering the potential barrier
questions.correct_option: The depletion region narrows, lowering the potential barrier
questions.explanation: Forward bias applies positive voltage to the p-side and negative to the n-side, opposing the built-in electric field and narrowing the space-charge layer.

questions.question: What happens to the depletion region width when a p-n junction diode is reverse biased?
options: The depletion region widens, increasing the potential barrier
The depletion region collapses to zero
Mobile charge carriers flood the junction
questions.answer: The depletion region widens, increasing the potential barrier
questions.correct_option: The depletion region widens, increasing the potential barrier
questions.explanation: Reverse bias reinforces the internal built-in field, pulling majority carriers away from the metallurgical junction and widening the depletion zone.

questions.question: What is the mathematical equation governing the current-voltage relationship of an ideal p-n junction diode (Shockley Diode Equation)?
questions.answer: I = I_s * [exp(qV / (η * k * T)) - 1]
questions.correct_option: I = I_s * [exp(qV / (η * k * T)) - 1]
questions.explanation: The Shockley equation describes diode diffusion current: I = I_s [exp(V / (η V_T)) - 1], where V_T = kT/q is the thermal voltage.

questions.question: What is the approximate value of the thermal voltage V_T = (k * T) / q at room temperature (T = 300 K)?
questions.answer: Approximately 25.9 mV (≈ 26 mV)
questions.correct_option: Approximately 25.9 mV (≈ 26 mV)

questions.question: What is the ideality factor (emission coefficient) η for an ideal germanium diode and a silicon diode at moderate forward bias?
options: η ≈ 1 for Ge, and η ≈ 1 to 2 for Si
questions.answer: η ≈ 1 for Ge, and η ≈ 1 to 2 for Si
questions.correct_option: η ≈ 1 for Ge, and η ≈ 1 to 2 for Si
questions.explanation: Germanium current is dominated by diffusion (η ≈ 1), while silicon exhibits both diffusion and recombination currents, making η between 1 and 2.

questions.question: What is the dynamic (ac) resistance r_d of a forward-biased diode mathematically defined as?
questions.answer: r_d = dV / dI = (η * V_T) / I_D
questions.correct_option: r_d = dV / dI = (η * V_T) / I_D
questions.explanation: Dynamic resistance is the reciprocal of the slope of the forward V-I characteristic: r_d = dV/dI ≈ η V_T / I_D.

questions.question: If a forward-biased silicon diode (η = 1) carries a DC current of I_D = 2.6 mA at room temperature, what is its dynamic AC resistance?
questions.explanation: r_d = V_T / I_D = 26 mV / 2.6 mA = 10 Ω.

questions.question: How does the static (DC) resistance R_DC = V_D / I_D compare to the dynamic (AC) resistance r_d in the forward conduction region?
options: R_DC is significantly larger than r_d (R_DC > r_d)
R_DC is much smaller than r_d
R_DC and r_d are always strictly equal
r_d is infinite while R_DC is zero
questions.answer: R_DC is significantly larger than r_d (R_DC > r_d)
questions.correct_option: R_DC is significantly larger than r_d (R_DC > r_d)
questions.explanation: Because the forward current increases exponentially, the tangent slope (dI/dV) is much steeper than the secant slope (I/V), meaning r_d < R_DC.

questions.question: What carriers constitute the tiny reverse saturation current I_s in a reverse-biased p-n junction?
options: Thermally generated minority carriers (electrons in p-region and holes in n-region)
Free electrons in the copper connecting wires
questions.answer: Thermally generated minority carriers (electrons in p-region and holes in n-region)
questions.correct_option: Thermally generated minority carriers (electrons in p-region and holes in n-region)
questions.explanation: Reverse bias sweeps minority carriers that diffuse to the edge of the depletion zone across the junction, creating the reverse saturation current I_s.

questions.question: How does the reverse saturation current I_s of a silicon diode change with increasing temperature?
options: I_s approximately doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature
I_s decreases by half for every 10°C
questions.answer: I_s approximately doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature
questions.correct_option: I_s approximately doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature
questions.explanation: Thermal generation of electron-hole pairs increases exponentially with temperature: I_s(T2) ≈ I_s(T1) * 2^((T2-T1)/10).

questions.question: How does the forward barrier voltage (cut-in voltage) of a silicon diode shift with temperature?
options: It decreases by approximately 2 mV per °C rise (-2 mV/°C)
It increases by 2 mV per °C rise (+2 mV/°C)
questions.answer: It decreases by approximately 2 mV per °C rise (-2 mV/°C)
questions.correct_option: It decreases by approximately 2 mV per °C rise (-2 mV/°C)
questions.explanation: dV/dT ≈ -2.0 to -2.5 mV/°C for silicon. As temperature rises, higher intrinsic carrier density allows forward current conduction at lower applied voltages.

questions.question: What is Zener breakdown in a heavily doped p-n junction diode?
options: Direct quantum mechanical tunneling of valence electrons into the conduction band under a very strong electric field (> 10⁶ V/cm)
Collisional impact ionization of lattice atoms
questions.answer: Direct quantum mechanical tunneling of valence electrons into the conduction band under a very strong electric field (> 10⁶ V/cm)
questions.correct_option: Direct quantum mechanical tunneling of valence electrons into the conduction band under a very strong electric field (> 10⁶ V/cm)
questions.explanation: In heavily doped junctions with narrow depletion width (< 10 nm), reverse voltage creates an intense field (> 10⁶ V/m) that enables direct quantum tunneling (Zener effect).

questions.question: How does Avalanche breakdown differ physically from Zener breakdown?
options: Avalanche breakdown is caused by impact ionization (accelerated carriers knocking valence electrons free), occurring at higher reverse voltages (> 5-6 V)
Avalanche breakdown occurs only at 0 V
Avalanche breakdown occurs in forward bias
Avalanche breakdown is caused by quantum tunneling
questions.answer: Avalanche breakdown is caused by impact ionization (accelerated carriers knocking valence electrons free), occurring at higher reverse voltages (> 5-6 V)
questions.correct_option: Avalanche breakdown is caused by impact ionization (accelerated carriers knocking valence electrons free), occurring at higher reverse voltages (> 5-6 V)
questions.explanation: In moderately/lightly doped diodes with wider depletion regions, minority carriers accelerate to high kinetic energies, colliding with lattice atoms to liberate secondary electron-hole pairs.

questions.question: What is the temperature coefficient of breakdown voltage for a Zener breakdown mechanism (< 5 V) vs an Avalanche breakdown mechanism (> 6 V)?
options: Zener has a negative temperature coefficient; Avalanche has a positive temperature coefficient
Zener is positive; Avalanche is negative
questions.answer: Zener has a negative temperature coefficient; Avalanche has a positive temperature coefficient
questions.correct_option: Zener has a negative temperature coefficient; Avalanche has a positive temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: Zener tunneling increases with temperature (narrowing bandgap), so V_Z drops (negative tempco). In avalanche, increased lattice vibrations impede carrier acceleration, requiring higher voltage (positive tempco).

questions.question: At approximately what breakdown voltage does a Zener diode exhibit near-zero temperature coefficient?
questions.answer: Around 5.1 V to 5.6 V
questions.correct_option: Around 5.1 V to 5.6 V
questions.explanation: Around 5.1 V to 5.6 V, the negative tempco of Zener tunneling and the positive tempco of avalanche multiplication precisely cancel each other, providing temperature-stable voltage references.

questions.question: What is the primary electronic application of a Zener diode operated in its reverse breakdown region?
options: Voltage regulation and voltage reference stabilization
questions.answer: Voltage regulation and voltage reference stabilization
questions.correct_option: Voltage regulation and voltage reference stabilization
questions.explanation: Because voltage remains virtually constant over a wide range of reverse breakdown current, Zener diodes maintain stable DC reference voltages.

questions.question: Why must a current-limiting resistor always be placed in series with a diode during forward V-I characterization?
options: To prevent excessive forward current that would cause catastrophic thermal burnout once knee voltage is exceeded
To reduce the input voltage to zero
To convert alternating current into radio waves
questions.answer: To prevent excessive forward current that would cause catastrophic thermal burnout once knee voltage is exceeded
questions.correct_option: To prevent excessive forward current that would cause catastrophic thermal burnout once knee voltage is exceeded
questions.explanation: Above the knee voltage, dynamic resistance drops to a few ohms; without a series ballast resistor, current would spike uncontrollably and destroy the junction.

questions.question: What is the transition (depletion-layer) capacitance C_T of a reverse-biased p-n junction diode?
options: C_T = ε * A / W (acts like a parallel-plate capacitor whose plate separation W widens with reverse voltage)
C_T is zero in reverse bias
C_T increases linearly with reverse voltage
questions.answer: C_T = ε * A / W (acts like a parallel-plate capacitor whose plate separation W widens with reverse voltage)
questions.correct_option: C_T = ε * A / W (acts like a parallel-plate capacitor whose plate separation W widens with reverse voltage)
questions.explanation: The unneutralized immobile ion sheets act as capacitor plates separated by the dielectric depletion region W: C_T ∝ 1 / √(V_bi + V_R).

questions.question: What specialized diode utilizes the voltage-variable transition capacitance of a reverse-biased junction for electronic radio frequency tuning?
questions.answer: Varactor (Varicap) diode
questions.correct_option: Varactor (Varicap) diode
questions.explanation: Varactor diodes are fabricated to maximize transition capacitance variation with reverse voltage, serving as voltage-controlled capacitors in RF VCOs and phase-locked loops.

questions.question: What is diffusion capacitance C_D in a p-n junction diode?
options: Capacitance caused by the time-delay storage of excess minority carrier charge in the neutral regions under forward bias
Capacitance of the depletion layer in reverse bias
questions.answer: Capacitance caused by the time-delay storage of excess minority carrier charge in the neutral regions under forward bias
questions.correct_option: Capacitance caused by the time-delay storage of excess minority carrier charge in the neutral regions under forward bias
questions.explanation: Under forward bias, minority carriers are injected across the junction and stored before recombining: C_D = (τ * I_D) / (η * V_T), scaling linearly with forward current.

questions.question: What is the reverse recovery time (t_rr) of a p-n junction diode?
options: The time required for stored minority carriers to be removed when switching rapidly from forward conduction to reverse bias
The time taken for a diode to cool down
The time to reach breakdown voltage
The time for current to reach 100 A
questions.answer: The time required for stored minority carriers to be removed when switching rapidly from forward conduction to reverse bias
questions.correct_option: The time required for stored minority carriers to be removed when switching rapidly from forward conduction to reverse bias
questions.explanation: When switched from forward to reverse, stored excess minority carriers must recombine or be swept out before the diode can block reverse current, causing a transient reverse current spike.

questions.question: Why are Schottky diodes capable of switching much faster than conventional silicon p-n junction diodes?
options: They are metal-semiconductor majority carrier devices with zero minority carrier storage and near-zero reverse recovery time (t_rr ≈ 0)
They have a wider depletion zone
questions.answer: They are metal-semiconductor majority carrier devices with zero minority carrier storage and near-zero reverse recovery time (t_rr ≈ 0)
questions.correct_option: They are metal-semiconductor majority carrier devices with zero minority carrier storage and near-zero reverse recovery time (t_rr ≈ 0)
questions.explanation: Schottky diodes use a metal-semiconductor barrier where conduction is carried solely by majority carriers, eliminating minority carrier storage delay.

questions.question: What is the typical forward voltage drop of a Schottky barrier diode?
questions.answer: Approximately 0.2 V to 0.4 V
questions.correct_option: Approximately 0.2 V to 0.4 V
questions.explanation: Metal-semiconductor barriers have a lower barrier height than silicon p-n junctions, providing a lower forward drop (~0.3 V) that minimizes power dissipation.

questions.question: In a Light Emitting Diode (LED), what physical process generates photon emission?
options: Radiative recombination of injected electrons and holes across the direct bandgap
Thermal blackbody radiation from wire heating
questions.answer: Radiative recombination of injected electrons and holes across the direct bandgap
questions.correct_option: Radiative recombination of injected electrons and holes across the direct bandgap
questions.explanation: Under forward bias, electrons and holes recombine radiatively across the direct energy gap, releasing energy as a photon of wavelength λ = hc / E_g.

questions.question: Why are direct bandgap semiconductors (such as GaAs, GaN, InP) used for LEDs rather than indirect bandgap semiconductors like Silicon?
options: In direct bandgap materials, electrons and holes can recombine directly without requiring phonon (lattice vibration) momentum conservation
Silicon absorbs all visible light completely
Direct bandgap materials have zero resistance
questions.answer: In direct bandgap materials, electrons and holes can recombine directly without requiring phonon (lattice vibration) momentum conservation
questions.correct_option: In direct bandgap materials, electrons and holes can recombine directly without requiring phonon (lattice vibration) momentum conservation
questions.explanation: In direct bandgap semiconductors, the conduction band minimum aligns with the valence band maximum in k-space, permitting high-probability radiative transitions without phonon assistance.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the peak emitted wavelength λ of an LED and its semiconductor bandgap energy E_g?
options: λ ≈ (h * c) / E_g = 1240 / E_g (where E_g is in eV and λ in nm)
questions.answer: λ ≈ (h * c) / E_g = 1240 / E_g (where E_g is in eV and λ in nm)
questions.correct_option: λ ≈ (h * c) / E_g = 1240 / E_g (where E_g is in eV and λ in nm)
questions.explanation: E = hν = hc/λ. Expressing E_g in electron-volts and λ in nanometers gives the convenient relation λ(nm) ≈ 1240 / E_g(eV).

questions.question: A red LED emits light at a peak wavelength of λ = 650 nm. What is the approximate energy bandgap E_g of its semiconductor material?
A blue LED based on Gallium Nitride (GaN) emits light at 450 nm. What is its approximate cut-in / knee voltage?
questions.answer: 2.7 V to 3.0 V
questions.correct_option: 2.7 V to 3.0 V
questions.explanation: Knee voltage scales with bandgap: V_knee ≈ E_g / q = 1240 / 450 nm ≈ 2.76 V.

questions.question: In which quadrant of the V-I coordinate plane does a solar cell operate when generating electrical power?
options: Fourth quadrant (positive voltage, negative current: delivering power to external load)
questions.answer: Fourth quadrant (positive voltage, negative current: delivering power to external load)
questions.correct_option: Fourth quadrant (positive voltage, negative current: delivering power to external load)
questions.explanation: A solar cell produces photo-generated current opposite to forward bias: with V > 0 and I < 0, the P = V * I product is negative, indicating power output.

questions.question: In which bias mode is a photodiode normally operated to achieve high speed and linear light-to-current response?
questions.answer: Reverse bias mode (photoconductive mode)
questions.correct_option: Reverse bias mode (photoconductive mode)
questions.explanation: Reverse bias expands the depletion width (decreasing junction capacitance for high bandwidth) and produces a reverse photocurrent that is strictly linear with incident light intensity.

questions.question: What is a Tunnel (Esaki) diode characterized by in its forward V-I curve?
options: A distinct Negative Differential Resistance (NDR) region where current decreases as voltage increases
A perfectly linear Ohm's law curve
questions.answer: A distinct Negative Differential Resistance (NDR) region where current decreases as voltage increases
questions.correct_option: A distinct Negative Differential Resistance (NDR) region where current decreases as voltage increases
questions.explanation: Degenerately doped p and n regions allow quantum tunneling at low forward voltages; as voltage increases, band overlap decreases, causing current to drop (negative resistance dI/dV < 0).

questions.question: What is the peak-to-valley current ratio (PVCR) in a Tunnel diode?
options: The ratio of the maximum forward tunneling peak current (I_P) to the minimum valley current (I_V)
The ratio of reverse to forward current
The ratio of breakdown voltage to knee voltage
The ratio of AC to DC resistance
questions.answer: The ratio of the maximum forward tunneling peak current (I_P) to the minimum valley current (I_V)
questions.correct_option: The ratio of the maximum forward tunneling peak current (I_P) to the minimum valley current (I_V)
questions.explanation: PVCR = I_P / I_V is a key figure of merit for tunnel diodes used in high-frequency microwave oscillators and fast pulse generators.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a freewheeling (flyback) diode connected in parallel with an inductive load (such as a relay coil)?
options: To suppress inductive high-voltage spikes (L * di/dt) when current is switched off by circulating current safely
To increase coil current during operation
To illuminate when the relay turns on
To step up DC voltage to AC
questions.answer: To suppress inductive high-voltage spikes (L * di/dt) when current is switched off by circulating current safely
questions.correct_option: To suppress inductive high-voltage spikes (L * di/dt) when current is switched off by circulating current safely
questions.explanation: When coil current is abruptly interrupted, V = -L(di/dt) can generate hundreds of volts; a reverse-parallel freewheeling diode clamps the spike to ~0.7 V, protecting switching transistors.

questions.question: What is the Ripple Factor of an ideal half-wave rectifier without a filter capacitor?
questions.explanation: Ripple factor γ = √( (V_rms / V_dc)² - 1 ). For half-wave rectification (V_rms = V_m/2, V_dc = V_m/π), γ = √( (π/2)² - 1 ) = √(2.467 - 1) = 1.211.

questions.question: What is the Ripple Factor of a full-wave bridge rectifier without a filter capacitor?
questions.explanation: For full-wave rectification, V_rms = V_m / √2, V_dc = 2V_m / π. Ripple factor γ = √( (π / (2√2))² - 1 ) = √(1.2337 - 1) ≈ 0.482.

questions.question: What is the Peak Inverse Voltage (PIV) rating required for the diodes in a full-wave bridge rectifier?
questions.answer: PIV = V_m (peak secondary voltage)
questions.correct_option: PIV = V_m (peak secondary voltage)
questions.explanation: In a bridge rectifier, the two non-conducting diodes in series share the reverse voltage, so each diode experiences a maximum reverse voltage equal to V_m.

questions.question: In a center-tapped full-wave rectifier, what is the Peak Inverse Voltage (PIV) across each non-conducting diode?
questions.answer: PIV = 2 * V_m
questions.correct_option: PIV = 2 * V_m
questions.explanation: When one diode conducts, the non-conducting diode experiences the full secondary end-to-end voltage: PIV = 2 * V_m.

questions.question: Why does a silicon diode conduct negligible current below its knee voltage (~0.6 V)?
options: The built-in electric field at the junction opposes majority carrier diffusion until external voltage overcomes it
Silicon atoms have no free electrons at room temperature
The series resistance is infinite at low voltage
Light emission absorbs all incoming energy
questions.answer: The built-in electric field at the junction opposes majority carrier diffusion until external voltage overcomes it
questions.correct_option: The built-in electric field at the junction opposes majority carrier diffusion until external voltage overcomes it
questions.explanation: The internal contact potential creates an electrostatic energy barrier; only carriers with thermal energy exceeding q(V_0 - V) can cross, which is negligible until V approaches V_0.

questions.question: What instrument is used in the laboratory to simultaneously plot the complete dynamic forward and reverse V-I curve of a diode on an oscilloscope?
options: A Curve Tracer (or dual-channel oscilloscope with XY Lissajous mode)
A digital multimeter set to resistance
questions.answer: A Curve Tracer (or dual-channel oscilloscope with XY Lissajous mode)
questions.correct_option: A Curve Tracer (or dual-channel oscilloscope with XY Lissajous mode)
questions.explanation: A curve tracer or an XY oscilloscope setup applies an AC sweep voltage across the diode while measuring voltage across the diode (X) and current across a sense resistor (Y).

questions.question: In an experimental circuit measuring diode forward V-I characteristics, why is the voltmeter connected directly across the diode rather than across the power supply?
options: To avoid including the voltage drop across the current-measuring ammeter and series resistor
To prevent blowing the voltmeter fuse
Because power supplies cannot be measured
questions.answer: To avoid including the voltage drop across the current-measuring ammeter and series resistor
questions.correct_option: To avoid including the voltage drop across the current-measuring ammeter and series resistor
questions.explanation: Connecting the voltmeter directly across the diode terminals ensures it measures true junction potential V_D without parasitic drops from the ammeter internal shunt resistance.

questions.question: If a diode forward current increases from 10 mA to 30 mA while voltage increases from 0.70 V to 0.73 V, what is the experimental dynamic resistance r_d?
What is the maximum theoretical efficiency of an ideal full-wave rectifier with resistive load and no capacitor?
questions.explanation: Maximum efficiency η_max = P_dc / P_ac = (8 / π²) ≈ 81.16% for full-wave rectification (twice that of half-wave at 40.6%).

questions.question: What is thermal runaway in a power diode?
options: A positive feedback loop where temperature rise increases reverse leakage current, causing higher power dissipation and further heating until destruction
The diode melting due to electrostatic charge
questions.answer: A positive feedback loop where temperature rise increases reverse leakage current, causing higher power dissipation and further heating until destruction
questions.correct_option: A positive feedback loop where temperature rise increases reverse leakage current, causing higher power dissipation and further heating until destruction
questions.explanation: Because I_s doubles every 10°C, leakage power dissipation P = V_R * I_s heats the junction. If heat cannot dissipate fast enough, temperature climbs uncontrollably until thermal breakdown.

questions.question: What is the bandgap of standard monocrystalline silicon at 300 K?
questions.explanation: Silicon has an indirect energy bandgap of E_g ≈ 1.12 eV at 300 K.

questions.question: What is the bandgap of germanium at room temperature (300 K)?
questions.explanation: Germanium has an indirect energy bandgap of approximately 0.66 eV at 300 K.

questions.question: What happens to the built-in potential barrier V_0 if the donor doping concentration N_D and acceptor doping concentration N_A are increased?
options: V_0 increases logarithmically according to V_0 = V_T * ln(N_A * N_D / n_i²)
questions.answer: V_0 increases logarithmically according to V_0 = V_T * ln(N_A * N_D / n_i²)
questions.correct_option: V_0 increases logarithmically according to V_0 = V_T * ln(N_A * N_D / n_i²)
questions.explanation: Higher doping pushes the Fermi levels closer to the band edges in both p and n regions, increasing built-in potential V_0 = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D / n_i²).

questions.question: What is a PIN diode and what is its primary high-frequency application?
options: A diode with an intrinsic (undoped) layer between p and n regions, functioning as an RF variable resistor or fast optical detector
A diode with three p-type terminals
A diode that conducts only when pinned to ground
A diode that replaces vacuum tubes in audio
questions.answer: A diode with an intrinsic (undoped) layer between p and n regions, functioning as an RF variable resistor or fast optical detector
questions.correct_option: A diode with an intrinsic (undoped) layer between p and n regions, functioning as an RF variable resistor or fast optical detector
questions.explanation: The thick intrinsic (I) layer yields low junction capacitance and long carrier lifetime, allowing the PIN diode to behave as an RF attenuator/switch whose resistance is tuned by DC bias.

questions.question: Why does an LED require a series resistor when connected to a DC supply voltage V_cc > V_knee?
options: Because its steep exponential V-I slope would allow destructive current overcurrent without external resistance
To step down the frequency of light
To make the LED shine in both directions
questions.answer: Because its steep exponential V-I slope would allow destructive current overcurrent without external resistance
questions.correct_option: Because its steep exponential V-I slope would allow destructive current overcurrent without external resistance
questions.explanation: Once the applied voltage exceeds the LED forward knee voltage, resistance drops near zero; the series resistor sets safe forward current: R = (V_cc - V_LED) / I_desired.
